messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Raymond, a 53-year-old married bus driver of North American background, came to treatment after more than a year of feeling that his life had narrowed around one night he could not escape. The assault happened after a late shift, when he was already exhausted and had agreed to give a coworker a ride home. He remembered the ordinary weight of the evening at first — the bus emptying out, the low hum of the engine, the radio crackling faintly — and then the sudden terror of being overpowered and raped. What has stayed with him most is not only what happened, but how vividly it comes back. When he remembers it, he said, it is not like thinking about an old event; it is as if the same terror returns in his body, and the memory runs through his mind like a film that will not stop playing. Certain sounds can still pull him straight back into it, especially noises that resemble the sounds from that night, and when he is already tired the recollection feels even closer, more immediate, as if fatigue leaves less distance between the present and the past.

In the weeks that followed, Raymond found himself watching for any sign that something similar could happen again. He had come to believe that people cannot be trusted and that whatever faith he had once placed in others, in life, or in a higher power had been badly broken. He was ashamed of what had happened to his body, and that shame colored the way he thought about the assault and about himself. Because of that, he became wary in situations that reminded him of the attack. Driving with others, once part of his job and something he had done without thought, now felt unsafe and exposing; being seated behind the wheel with a passenger nearby made him scan the seats, mirrors, and faces with a vigilance that left him tense and uneasy. Related sounds on the bus — a sudden laugh, a scuffle near the back, the metallic click of a seatbelt, a tone that echoed the night of the assault — could make him feel cornered before he had time to reason with himself. Those moments were not just reminders; they fed his mistrust, confirming for him that other people might turn dangerous without warning, and that he could not count on anyone to protect him.

That mistrust then shaped the way the memory itself returned. When Raymond noticed a passenger behind him, or heard a sound that resembled the assault, his mind would snap back to the event with the same terror attached. He described the recollection as if it arrived whole, not softened by time, bringing back the humiliation and fear together. The shame on recall was especially painful: remembering did not simply mean reliving the violence, but confronting what had been done to his body and the sense that he had been left altered by it. In those moments he would become even more alert to possible danger, listening harder, looking more often in the mirrors, and bracing for the next sign that someone could hurt him again. The more he searched for threat, the more the bus and the people on it felt charged with it.

Over months, Raymond began arranging his life around these moments. He tried to avoid being tired because exhaustion made the memories sharper, but his work schedule often left him drained anyway, and on those days the echoes came more easily. He started taking routes and breaks with more caution, and his interactions with riders became clipped and guarded. The changes at work were obvious enough that his wife noticed he came home worn down and withdrawn, as if he had spent the day fighting something invisible. He was embarrassed that he could no longer occupy the role of the steady professional he had once taken pride in. At home, he carried the same belief that people could not be trusted, and that belief kept the circle tight: the less safe others seemed, the more he monitored them; the more he monitored, the more often he noticed the sounds and situations that stirred the memory; and each return of the memory deepened his shame and conviction that the world was no longer dependable.

By the time he sought help, Raymond was frightened by how completely the assault had shaped the way he moved through his days. He had reached a point where he was most afraid that driving tired, with passengers behind him and the wrong sound in the bus, would pull him back into the terror again and again, and he was also afraid that he would keep retreating from other people until distrust became the only way he knew how to live. He came to treatment hoping to find some way to sit in the driver’s seat, hear an ordinary sound, and no longer feel the night closing in on him.
